opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the central questions right now. If you look at where models fall short, it's usually not that they can't do any individual step. It's that they have trouble stringing a lot of steps together coherently over a long period. They lose track of what they were doing, they don't recover well from mistakes, and they don't really get better at the task as they go the way a person would.

Memory matters on a few levels. The simplest is just context: having the relevant history of what you've done available so you can refer back to it. Longer context windows have helped a lot, but just having tokens in the window isn't the same as using them well. The model has to know what's important, what it already tried, and what the current state of the problem is.

Then there's something more like learning on the job. When a person starts a new project, the first few days they're slow, and then they build up a model of the codebase or the domain and get much more efficient. Right now our models mostly don't do that. Each episode starts more or less fresh. So I think there's a lot of room for some combination of better in-context learning, some kind of persistent memory or notes the model maintains, and maybe at some point actually updating weights during deployment.

On the training side, I think the big lever is training on longer-horizon tasks directly with RL, where the model has to accomplish something that takes many steps and gets feedback on whether it succeeded. That teaches skills that are hard to get from next-token prediction alone, like noticing you've gone down the wrong path and backtracking, or checking your own work. My guess is that once models are trained more on these long tasks, a fair amount of the coherence problem improves, because a lot of it is just a lack of practice rather than a fundamental limitation.

So, short answer: memory gives you the raw material to stay coherent, and learning, both during training and ideally at deployment time, is what lets the model actually use it and improve over a long task.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning on the job and maintaining persistent memory or notes, and says learning during deployment can help models improve over a long task.

r002.rationale: It mentions memory at several levels, from context to persistent memory, but does not describe short-term and long-term memory as lying on a continuum.

r003.rationale: It says longer context windows have helped a lot and that having relevant task history available supports coherence over long tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the big open problems right now. If you look at what current systems are good at, it's tasks where you can hold everything you need in the context window, and the task is over in a few minutes. Things fall apart when you get to tasks that take hours or days, where you need to remember what you tried before, what worked, what didn't, and where the environment is changing underneath you.

The way I think about it, there are really two different things going on. One is memory in the narrow sense, which is just retaining information across a long task. You can get pretty far with that by having the model write things down, keep notes, maintain some kind of scratchpad or external store. That's a bit of an engineering problem and people are making progress on it.

The more interesting thing is learning, in the sense of actually getting better at the task while you're doing it. If I hand a new person a job, they're not very good on day one, but after a few weeks they've picked up all these little things about how the codebase works, what the team cares about, which approaches tend to fail. Current models don't really do that. Every time you start a new session, you're starting from the same weights, with the same priors, and all that accumulated experience is gone unless you've explicitly stuffed it into the prompt.

So I think the frontier is figuring out how to close that loop. Some of it could be in-context, where the model gets good enough at using its own notes that it effectively learns from them. Some of it might be lighter-weight fine-tuning, where you actually update the model based on experience in a particular deployment. And a big part of it is just the RL training itself, training on much longer horizon tasks so the model learns the meta-skill of managing its own state, noticing when it's confused, going back and checking its work. Humans aren't born knowing how to do a multi-month project either. We learn how to break things down, how to keep track of progress, and I think a lot of that is learnable from experience in the same way.

r001.rationale: The response says models need to get better at a task while doing it and describes retaining and updating notes or an external store across a long task.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes memory from learning but does not describe short-term and long-term memory as lying on a continuum.

r003.rationale: It mentions the context window as useful for tasks lasting a few minutes, but does not say that putting information into a long context can substantially support long-horizon tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two different things that matter here. One is learning how to carry out a long task: how to break it into pieces, recognize when an approach isn’t working, and recover from mistakes. The other is keeping track of what’s happened during this particular task. What have you tried? What did you discover? What are you still uncertain about?

You could have a system that’s very good at each individual step, but if it loses track of those things, it’ll repeat work or go down a path it already ruled out. So memory needs to preserve the information that will actually affect later decisions. That’s harder than just keeping a transcript, because eventually the transcript becomes too large to use effectively.

And these two things interact. The system can learn what’s worth remembering and when to retrieve it. Ideally, an experience helps it finish the current task, but also improves how it approaches similar tasks in the future. I think getting that feedback loop to work reliably is a big part of making systems useful over longer time horizons.

r001.rationale: It describes tracking what happened during the current task and learning from experience to improve the approach, including as the task unfolds.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes information retained for the current task from learning that improves future tasks, but does not describe short-term and long-term memory as a continuum.

r003.rationale: It says a transcript can become too large to use effectively and emphasizes selective memory; it does not state that putting information into a long context can substantially support long-horizon tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two things that help. One is learning how to make progress over a long horizon: breaking the problem down, recognizing when you’re stuck, and deciding when to try a different approach. The other is remembering enough about what you’ve already done that you don’t keep repeating the same mistakes.

You can get some of that memory just by keeping a record in the context, or having the system write notes that it can retrieve later. But there’s also a question of what should get incorporated into the model’s weights. If you discover a useful strategy on one task, ideally that improves how you approach similar tasks in the future.

The tricky part is that a long task gives you a lot of experience, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you which decisions were good. You might succeed despite making several bad decisions, or fail after doing almost everything right. So memory helps preserve the experience, and learning has to turn that experience into something useful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning from experience and recording or retrieving notes, but does not clearly state that both learning and memory must be updated during the task.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes context or notes from incorporating information into model weights, but does not describe short-term and long-term memory as a continuum.

r003.rationale: It mentions keeping a record in context, but does not say that a long context can go a substantial way toward supporting long-horizon tasks.
